editorial_reason: The internal Hom definition relies on general modules, linear homomorphisms and their pointwise operations. The reconstructed registry has no suitable independent basic module or generic linear-map definition; specialised Hom-derived constructions are downstream.
source_text: For modules M,N over a commutative ring R, the internal Hom Hom_R(M,N) is the R-module of R-linear homomorphisms M→N, with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication (r·f)(m)=r·f(m).

editorial_reason: This connecting homomorphism depends on kernels, cokernels and exact diagrams of abelian groups. No generic kernel, cokernel or exact-sequence definition was independently acquired; specific Ext/Tor constructions cannot replace them.
source_text: For a commutative diagram of abelian groups with exact rows X→Y→Z→0 and 0→U→V→W and vertical maps α,β,γ, the snake connecting map ∂:ker(γ)→coker(α) sends z to the class of an element u∈U whose image in V equals β(y), where y∈Y maps to z; this class is independent of the choices.

editorial_reason: The lifting-property definition requires square-zero ideals, algebra homomorphisms and uniqueness of lifts. The other formally unramified formulation is already grouped under this same meaning, and no distinct suitable foundational concept is available.
source_text: A ring homomorphism R→S is formally unramified if, for every R-algebra A and square-zero ideal I⊆A, any R-algebra map S→A/I admits at most one lift to an R-algebra map S→A.

editorial_reason: The adjunction condition depends on arbitrary functors, Hom sets and naturality, but no suitable generic functor/natural-transformation meaning was reconstructed. Special monoidal or presheaf functors are not foundational substitutes.
source_text: For functors L:C to D and R:D to C, L is left adjoint to R when there are bijections between the morphisms L(X) to Y in D and X to R(Y) in C, natural in both X and Y.

editorial_reason: The general group object and multiplication/inversion structure are prerequisites for topological groups. There is no standalone abstract group definition; profinite groups and group actions are more specialised downstream notions.
source_text: A topological group is a group G with a topology under which the multiplication map G×G→G and inversion map G→G are both continuous.

editorial_reason: A topological ring combines arbitrary ring operations with continuity. A generic ring definition and underlying topological space definition are absent; specialised module and algebraic-geometry constructions depend on this concept rather than define it.
source_text: A topological ring is a ring R with a topology for which its addition R×R→R and multiplication R×R→R are continuous maps.

editorial_reason: This point relation is defined by closure of singletons in an arbitrary topological space. No general closure-of-a-set or topological-space meaning is independently supported; irreducible and constructible variants concern different constructions.
source_text: For points x and y in a topological space X, x is a specialization of y when x lies in the closure of the singleton {y}; equivalently y is a generalization of x.

editorial_reason: The cartesian lifting arrow can be defined for an arbitrary functor between categories; Grothendieck fibrations are a class of such functors, not a prerequisite for the arrow definition. A suitable general functor definition is missing.
source_text: For a functor p:E→C, a morphism φ:y→x in E is strongly p-cartesian if for every object z in E, each pair consisting of a map ψ:z→x and a base arrow p(z)→p(y) that composes with p(φ) to p(ψ) factors uniquely through φ.

editorial_reason: A topological basis is built from general open sets and topologies. No generic open-set or topological-space definition is screened; topology subbases and spectral-space bases are related derived notions rather than prerequisites.
source_text: For a topological space X, a basis is a family B of open sets such that, whenever an open U contains x, some member of B contains x and is itself contained in U.

editorial_reason: The action laws require an arbitrary group and its identity and product operations. A general abstract-group definition is absent; Galois and profinite groups concern more specialised groups and cannot supply it.
source_text: A left action of a group G on a set X is a map G×X→X such that e·x=x for all x and (gh)·x=g·(h·x) for every g,h∈G and x∈X.

editorial_reason: Geometric reducedness requires the general property that an algebra is a reduced ring after field extension. Only reduced schemes, not a basic reduced-ring definition, were reconstructed; these contexts cannot be conflated.
source_text: A k-algebra A is geometrically reduced if for every field extension K/k the tensor-product K-algebra A⊗_k K is a reduced ring.

editorial_reason: The preorder axioms require a generic binary relation on a set, but that foundational relation concept has no independent screened meaning. Partial orders and directed preorders are derived restrictions, not prerequisites for defining preorders.
source_text: A preordered set is a set I endowed with a reflexive and transitive binary relation ≤.

editorial_reason: Localization begins with an arbitrary commutative ring and a multiplicative subset. No stand-alone generic ring or multiplicative-subset definition is present; module and graded localizations are constructions using this one.
source_text: Given a commutative ring R and multiplicative subset S⊆R, the localization S^{-1}R is the ring of fractions r/s modulo (r,s)∼(r′,s′) if t(rs′−r′s)=0 for some t∈S.

editorial_reason: An extension field is specified by fields and an injective field homomorphism. General field and field-homomorphism definitions are not independently available; Galois or algebraic extensions are more restrictive derived cases.
source_text: An extension E/F of fields is an inclusion F⊆E of fields; equivalently, it is an injective field homomorphism F→E with the image identified as a subfield of E.

editorial_reason: A setoid is defined from an arbitrary groupoid and its automorphisms. No foundational general groupoid definition is available; fibred-in-groupoids and groupoid-valued presheaves are specialised contexts.
source_text: A setoid is a groupoid C in which every object has only its identity automorphism; equivalently, between two objects there is at most one arrow, and its existence is an equivalence relation.

editorial_reason: Bilinearity presupposes the ordinary module and R-linear-map notions. Neither has an independently screened general definition, and tensor products are universal objects built from bilinear maps, not their prerequisites.
source_text: For R-modules M,N,P, a map b:M×N→P is R-bilinear if it is R-linear in M when N is fixed and R-linear in N when M is fixed.

editorial_reason: A free resolution presupposes free modules, chain complexes and exactness. No foundational free-module or generic exact-chain-complex meaning is present; Tor and Ext are subsequently constructed using resolutions.
source_text: A free resolution of an R-module M is an exact augmented chain complex ⋯→F_2→F_1→F_0→M→0 with every F_i a free R-module.

editorial_reason: The Leibniz-law definition involves general ring maps, additive maps and module multiplication, but the basic ring/module structures have no suitable independent definitions. Kähler differentials are universal objects built from derivations.
source_text: For a ring map R→S and an S-module M, an R-derivation D:S→M is an additive map vanishing on the image of R and satisfying Leibniz's law D(ab)=aD(b)+bD(a).

editorial_reason: The geometric condition requires the underlying scalar-extension algebras to be integral domains. A general integral-domain meaning is missing; a normal integral domain and geometric integral closure tests cannot replace the basic domain prerequisite.
source_text: A k-algebra A is geometrically integral when, for every field extension K/k, the tensor-product algebra A⊗_k K is an integral domain.

editorial_reason: The strict-map condition compares quotient and subspace topologies for the image. Generic quotient topology and subspace topology have no independent screened meanings; submersive maps are a different restriction.
source_text: A continuous map f:X→Y is strict when the quotient topology from X on the image f(X) agrees with the subspace topology induced on f(X) from Y.

editorial_reason: Submersiveness is a surjective map carrying the quotient topology on its codomain. The generic quotient-topology construction is absent, and strict continuous maps need not be surjective, so neither is a prerequisite target.
source_text: A continuous map f:X→Y is submersive if it is surjective and Y has the quotient topology for f; equivalently, U⊆Y is open exactly when f^{-1}(U) is open in X.

editorial_reason: Integrality of an element is expressed by a monic polynomial over a general base ring. The registry lacks basic monic-polynomial and general ring definitions; integral closure and integral homomorphisms are defined using this notion.
source_text: For a ring homomorphism R→S, an element s of S is integral over R if s satisfies some monic polynomial with coefficients in the image of R.

editorial_reason: The Noetherian condition uses arbitrary ideals, their finite generators and inclusion chains. There is no separate general ideal definition in the reconstructed set; specialised Noetherian graded/topological notions are not prerequisites.
source_text: A commutative ring R is Noetherian if every ideal of R is finitely generated; equivalently, every ascending chain I_1⊆I_2⊆⋯ of ideals eventually stabilizes.

editorial_reason: A generic colimit is a universal cocone in a category. The foundational notions of category, functor and natural compatible cocone are not separately defined; finite and filtered colimits are special cases of this one.
source_text: For a diagram F:I→C, a colimit is an object Q equipped with compatible morphisms F(i)→Q such that every other cocone F(i)→Z factors uniquely through Q.

editorial_reason: A generic categorical limit requires an arbitrary category, diagram and cone. No generic category/functor meaning was independently reconstructed, and inverse limits, pullbacks and products are derived particular cases.
source_text: For a diagram F:I→C, a limit consists of an object L of C with arrows L→F(i) compatible with every arrow of I, such that each other compatible cone factors uniquely through L.

editorial_reason: The Jacobson radical is defined using all maximal ideals of the ring, but no general maximal-ideal definition is available. A Jacobson ring is a separate ring property rather than a prerequisite definition of maximal ideal.
source_text: For a commutative ring R, its Jacobson radical Jac(R) is the intersection of all maximal ideals of R.

editorial_reason: The equivalent Jacobson-radical test invokes invertible ring elements and their arithmetic. There is no basic unit/invertible-element meaning; its intersection-of-maximal-ideals version is already grouped in this same meaning.
source_text: Equivalently, an element x∈R belongs to Jac(R) exactly when 1−xy is invertible in R for every y∈R.

editorial_reason: Finite generation of an R-module depends on the basic module, linear-combination and span concepts. A general R-module definition is absent; finite presentation and projectivity are stronger downstream properties.
source_text: An R-module M is finitely generated if there exist m_1,…,m_n∈M such that M=Rm_1+⋯+Rm_n; equivalently there is a surjective homomorphism R^n→M for some finite n.

editorial_reason: A filtered category is described using arbitrary category objects, morphisms and equalization of parallel arrows. No suitable generic category or functor definition is present; filtered colimits are constructions indexed by these categories.
source_text: A category I is filtered if it is nonempty, any two objects admit arrows into a common object, and every pair of parallel arrows u,v:i⇉j can be equalized after an arrow j→k.

editorial_reason: The Jacobson-space condition refers to closed points, closed subsets and density in arbitrary topological spaces. General closed sets and closure/density have no basic separate screened meaning in this collection.
source_text: A topological space X is Jacobson if for each closed subset Z⊆X, the set of points of Z that are closed in X is dense in Z, so Z is its closure.

editorial_reason: Differential operators of finite order are defined inductively using linear maps, commutators and module scalar multiplication. The generic R-linear-map and module notions are absent; principal-parts modules are universal objects built from operators.
source_text: For a ring map R→S and S-modules M,N, an R-linear map D:M→N is a differential operator of order at most k if k=0 and D is S-linear, or if k>0 and for every s∈S the commutator m↦D(sm)−sD(m) has order at most k−1.

editorial_reason: The module length counts strict chains of arbitrary submodules. There is no generic submodule or module meaning in the independent corpus; simple-module and Artinian conditions are associated but do not define chains.
source_text: The length of an R-module M is the supremum of integers n for which M has a strictly increasing chain of R-submodules 0=M_0⊊M_1⊊⋯⊊M_n=M, with infinity if the possible lengths are unbounded.

editorial_reason: The annihilator ideal of a module requires a general module action and ideal of a ring, neither of which has an independently reconstructed foundational definition. The annihilator of an element is a related special case.
source_text: For an R-module M, its annihilator Ann_R(M) is the ideal consisting of r∈R for which r·m=0 for every m∈M.

editorial_reason: The annihilator of a module element uses the module action and the general notion of a ring ideal. Those basic concepts are missing; the whole-module annihilator instead quantifies over all elements and is not a prerequisite.
source_text: For m in an R-module M, its annihilator Ann_R(m) is the ideal {r∈R:r·m=0}.

editorial_reason: The infinitesimal lifting property uses general R-algebras and ideals with square zero, neither separately defined at the foundational level. Smooth and étale maps are stronger conditions, not prerequisites for formal smoothness.
source_text: A commutative ring homomorphism R→S is formally smooth if every R-algebra map S→A/I lifts to an R-algebra map S→A whenever A is an R-algebra and I⊆A satisfies I²=0.

editorial_reason: Extremal disconnectedness is stated by applying closure to every open subset. The general closure and open-set definitions are absent, while clopen-spectrum and connectedness entries are different context-specific properties.
source_text: A topological space X is extremally disconnected if the closure of every open subset U of X is itself an open subset of X.

editorial_reason: A locally closed partition relies on locally closed subsets of arbitrary topological spaces. The catalog has a locally closed immersion of schemes, but not the corresponding general topological-subset definition.
source_text: A partition of a topological space X in this setting is a decomposition X=⨆_{i∈I}X_i into pairwise disjoint locally closed subsets whose union is all of X.

editorial_reason: Local finiteness of a family uses arbitrary neighbourhoods of points and a generic indexed collection. The reconstructed corpus lacks generic neighbourhood and topology definitions; finite colimits and covers are different constructions.
source_text: A collection (E_i) of subsets of X is locally finite if every x∈X has an open neighbourhood meeting E_i for only finitely many indices i.

editorial_reason: The interior of a set is the largest open subset it contains. No suitable generic topological open-set or space definition is available; topological bases and nowhere-dense sets are downstream applications.
source_text: The interior Int_X(A) of a subset A of a topological space X is the union of all open subsets of X contained in A, equivalently the largest open subset of X lying in A.

editorial_reason: The source asks that scalar extensions be regular rings. A regular-local-ring meaning was reconstructed, but a general regular-ring meaning was not; relating these accurately requires verifying the local-to-global convention before choosing a target.
source_text: A Noetherian k-algebra R is geometrically regular over a field k if R⊗_k K is a regular ring for every finite field extension K/k; equivalently this holds for all field extensions K/k under the hypotheses of the Stacks criterion.

editorial_reason: Cofinality is stated for arbitrary well-ordered sets. Although von Neumann ordinals were reconstructed, a general well-order relation was not; restricting the domain to ordinals would silently narrow this definition.
source_text: A subset A of a well-ordered set T is cofinal if for every t∈T some a∈A satisfies t≤a.

editorial_reason: Finite type of a ring homomorphism relies on the basic R-algebra structure and algebra generators. No foundational algebra or ring-map meaning is independently supported; finite presentation is a stronger derived property.
source_text: A ring map R→S is of finite type if S can be generated as an R-algebra by finitely many elements, equivalently S is a quotient of R[x_1,…,x_n] for some finite n.

editorial_reason: A connected category is defined from paths or zigzags of arbitrary morphisms. The generic category and morphism definitions have not been reconstructed; connected topological spaces are a different context.
source_text: A category I is connected if it is nonempty and each pair of its objects can be joined by a finite sequence of morphisms whose directions may alternate.

editorial_reason: Roots of unity are defined using the multiplicative group of a field and the unit element. The current meanings lack generic group and field definitions; primitive nth roots are more restrictive examples.
source_text: An nth root of unity in a field F is an element ζ satisfying ζ^n=1; all such elements form a subgroup μ_n(F) of F×.

editorial_reason: Topological irreducibility uses proper closed subsets of arbitrary spaces. No general closed-set or topological-space meaning was acquired; geometric irreducibility of algebras is a specialised derived condition.
source_text: A nonempty topological space is irreducible if it cannot be expressed as the union of two proper closed subsets.

editorial_reason: A multiplicative system of arrows relies on the basic notion of a category, its morphisms and their composition. No suitable generic category definition was acquired; categorical localization is constructed from this notion.
source_text: A multiplicative system of arrows in a category contains all identities, is closed under composition, and satisfies both left and right Ore-square completion and the corresponding cancellation axioms.

editorial_reason: The coprime-polynomial condition uses ideals of the polynomial ring and the unit ideal. Generic ideals and polynomial rings are not independently defined; their common-root test is already an equivalent formulation here.
source_text: Polynomials f,g∈k[x] over a field k are relatively prime when the ideal (f,g) they generate is the entire polynomial ring k[x].

editorial_reason: The Hausdorff separation axiom refers to disjoint open neighbourhoods of points. General open sets and topological spaces have no basic meaning in this reconstruction; the closed-diagonal criterion is already part of this meaning.
source_text: A topological space X is Hausdorff if every pair of distinct points has disjoint open neighbourhoods.

editorial_reason: Equivalence of objects is stated for an arbitrary 2-category. Only strict 2-categories were independently defined; promoting the strict case as a universal prerequisite may incorrectly discard weak 2-categorical contexts.
source_text: Two objects X,Y in a 2-category are equivalent if there are 1-morphisms F:X→Y and G:Y→X with invertible 2-morphisms FG⇒id_Y and GF⇒id_X.

editorial_reason: A strict 2-category uses generic categories, functors and natural transformations at the hom level. No basic category/functor meaning is present; a (2,1)-category is a more restricted subclass, not a prerequisite.
source_text: A strict 2-category consists of objects, hom-categories whose objects are 1-morphisms and arrows are 2-morphisms, and strictly associative and unital composition functors between hom-categories satisfying the interchange law.

editorial_reason: This Stacks convention defines constructible subsets using retrocompact open subsets of arbitrary spaces. There is no independent retrocompact-open or generic topological-space meaning; Noetherian constructibility is a narrower convention.
source_text: A subset E of a topological space X is constructible if it is a finite union of sets U\V with U and V open and retrocompact in X.

editorial_reason: The source uses contravariant pseudofunctors valued in groupoids, whereas the acquired category-valued-presheaf definition specifies strict ordinary functors. Their relation needs pseudofunctor/coherence context review before inserting a dependency.
source_text: A groupoid-valued presheaf on a category C is a contravariant pseudofunctor assigning a groupoid F(U) to each object U of C and compatible pullback functors F(U)→F(V) to arrows V→U.

editorial_reason: Regular sequences require module quotients, injective scalar actions and nonzero quotients. A suitable basic module/submodule meaning was not independently recovered; quasi-regular sequences are not a substitute.
source_text: A finite sequence f_1,…,f_r in a ring R is M-regular for an R-module M if f_i acts injectively on M/(f_1,…,f_{i-1})M for every i and the final quotient M/(f_1,…,f_r)M is nonzero.

editorial_reason: A valuation ring is defined as an integral domain with a specified condition inside its fraction field. No general integral-domain or fraction-field meaning is present; a discrete valuation ring is a restricted downstream variant.
source_text: An integral domain V with fraction field K is a valuation ring if each nonzero x∈K has at least one of x and x^{-1} lying in V.

editorial_reason: Von Neumann ordinals require transitive sets and well-ordering by membership. The independent registry lacks foundational transitive-set and well-order definitions; successor and limit ordinals depend on this concept.
source_text: An ordinal is a transitive set α on which the membership relation ∈ is a well-order: each nonempty subset has an ∈-least element, and every member of α is itself a subset of α.

editorial_reason: The nonnegative grading definition uses a general ring and additive group direct sums. These general ring and abelian-group prerequisites were not independently acquired; graded modules depend on such rings.
source_text: A nonnegatively graded ring S is a direct sum S=⊕_{n≥0}S_n of additive groups satisfying S_nS_m⊆S_{n+m} for every n,m≥0.

editorial_reason: An opposite category reverses arrows and composition in an arbitrary category. No independent basic category/object/morphism meaning exists; contravariant and representable functors depend on the opposite construction.
source_text: For a category C, the opposite category C^op has the same objects as C and a morphism X→Y in C^op for each morphism Y→X in C, with composition reversed.
